title: Isfahan, half the world
hookLine: the Safavid capital, with its great square and blue-tiled mosques

lines: A SQUARE THE SIZE OF A TOWN.
A PALACE, A BAZAAR, BLUE MOSQUES.
cards: The people at the far end of the square look like grains of rice. That is how long it is. Fountains run down the middle.
Shops line every side, and on each side something different waits: a palace with a high porch where the shah could sit and watch, a bazaar gate, and mosques covered in blue.
Polo was once played on this ground, with goalposts at each end. Families still picnic on the grass at night. People in Iran have a rhyming saying about it: Esfahan, nesf-e jahan.

teach.h: NAQSH-E JAHAN: THE IMAGE OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: Isfahan became the capital of the Safavid shahs, and under Shah Abbas it was rebuilt around this great square, called Naqsh-e Jahan, the image of the world.
On the south side stands the Shah Mosque, now often called the Imam Mosque. Its gate faces the square. But walk through it and something odd happens: the building turns.
The square runs one way; the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, runs another.

teach.h: THE MOSQUE TURNS TO FACE MECCA.
teach.b: So the architects bent the entrance, and the mosque behind it swings around to face Mecca. The square belongs to the city. The prayer hall belongs to the qibla.
On the east side is a smaller mosque, named for Sheikh Lotfollah, a scholar.
It has no minarets and no great courtyard: one room under a dome, where the tiles climb in a pattern that narrows toward a center, and light from small windows falls across them.
Then the tiles everywhere: blue, turquoise, yellow, white, cut and fitted, or painted and fired, covering walls, arches and domes.
Qur'an verses in tall letters, flowers, vines, and patterns that repeat, rather than pictures of people or animals. Why so much beauty in a prayer room?

teach.h: GOD IS BEAUTIFUL AND LOVES BEAUTY.
teach.b: A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in Sahih Muslim, says that God is beautiful and loves beauty.
And the Qur'an says that to God belong the east and the west, and wherever you turn, there is the face of God.
A city called half the world, and a prayer hall that turned from it to face one point. Half the world.

how: Mosques from Morocco to Indonesia are often decorated with tilework, calligraphy of Qur'an verses and geometric and floral patterns, and a mosque's prayer hall is oriented toward the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca.

o: the Safavid capital, built around a vast square
a Persian name for any royal polo ground
a Persian word for a garden in four parts

s: the Shah Mosque lines up straight with the square
the gate faces the square, but the building turns to face the qibla.
the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque has no minarets
one room under a dome, with no minarets and no great courtyard.
the tiles are full of pictures of people
they carry Qur'an verses, flowers, vines and patterns, with no people or animals.

games.q: you're the architect. the shah's square runs one way. the qibla, toward Mecca, runs another. the mosque has to sit on the square. what do you do?
o: line the mosque up with the square and ignore the qibla.
face the gate to the square and turn the building toward Mecca.
games.why: the gate faces the square, and the entrance bends so the prayer hall faces Mecca. the square belongs to the city; the prayer hall belongs to the qibla.

practice: Find a photo of the Sheikh Lotfollah dome or the Shah Mosque gate, or look at anything blue near you: a mug, the sky, a shirt.

Let your eyes move slowly from the edge toward the center, the way the pattern climbs the dome, noticing where it repeats and where it changes. If you pray, you can let the beauty turn you toward God.
